title: Economic and affordability salience can coexist with divided party attribution and weak policy representation
source_unit: Pew Research Center July 2026 survey of economic salience, party fit, presidential attribution, and AI-policy representation
geography: United States; 3,554 adults including 2,779 registered voters

observations.period: July 6-12, 2026; Pew survey field window approaching the 2026 midterms

denominator.unit: U.S. adults; 2,779 registered voters for election-specific items and question-specific bases vary

economy_issue_salience.unit: percent of registered voters naming the economy as the issue they most want congressional candidates to discuss; 15% name cost of living or affordability

party_economic_fit.value: 37% say Democrats do a better job handling economic issues and 36% say Republicans

presidential_vote_framing.value: 42% say their midterm vote is mainly against Trump, 22% mainly for Trump, and 35% say Trump is not much of a factor

ai_policy_representation.unit: percent saying neither party represents them well on AI policy

material_recovery.unit: missing respondent-level price, wage, employment, debt, care, enacted-policy, household-remedy, and recovery outcomes

mechanism.value: Material concerns can become politically salient without producing a single responsible actor or a strong representation channel: economic attribution is nearly balanced, presidential framing is divided, and AI policy has a large neither-party response

observations.method: Structured extraction from Pew Research Center aggregate estimates of campaign issue demand, party issue fit, presidential attribution, election attention, congressional favorability, and AI-policy representation; political judgment is kept separate from household exposure and validated action.
observations.uncertainty: This is a cross-sectional self-reported survey, not a household economic panel, causal voting estimate, forecast, validated ballot record, or policy-implementation study. Individual exposure, prior judgment, information source, campaign contact, policy knowledge, and later behavior are not retained.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults and registered voters with question-specific party and issue subgroups; subgroup bases and sampling details are not reproduced here.
observations.counterinterpretation: Economic salience may reflect national discourse or generalized concern rather than a respondent's own dated material shock; vote framing may express identity or coalition choice rather than a specific economic judgment.

boundary: This record establishes a dated cross-sectional bridge from economic and affordability salience to political attribution and representation. It does not establish a material shock, causal vote effect, policy delivery, household recovery, trust change, or geopolitical consequence.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The hash covers the compact project event ledger derived from Pew's published aggregate survey report; respondent microdata, household records, validated vote files, and policy implementation records are not retained.
